Cloud tasking first reasoned review (2026-10-23)

Identification and provenance
These three source programs reconstruct the suffix-dispatched cloud-file .NET
RAT described at https://securelist.com/uefi-bootkit-blackx/121539/ (22 Oct 2026).
The C# comment explicitly says this is not recovered BlackX source. Python and
PowerShell identify themselves as variants of the reported protocol. The local
testdata/cloud-managed-tasking-evidence.txt makes the same source-only limit.
No original-family, bootkit, driver, actor, or deployment attribution is made.
Hashes of all supplied samples were checked and agree with the user input.

Judgement: MALICIOUS for each functional backdoor reconstruction.
The decisive behavior is cloud-controlled arbitrary managed-code invocation,
with the invocation result returned through cloud storage. C# additionally
exports remotely selected local files and accepts remotely selected file writes.
These are reusable backdoor handlers rather than mere HTTP or reflection APIs.
Comments/test-token wording and source-only packaging support a legitimate
research explanation. Authorized lab use could explain possession; the supplied
context does not establish such deployment authorization or a containment harness.
The verdict concerns the implementations' backdoor behavior, not an assertion
that these files were deployed by the actor in the report.

Execution paths and effects
Python: at module load, sys.argv[1] becomes a Graph Bearer header. An infinite
loop requests /root/children, selects filenames ending in 0x01, fetches the
selected item content, converts response bytes with bytearray, loads them via
Assembly.Load, resolves TEST.Class1.RunCMD, and invokes it with an empty string
array. str(result).encode() becomes a PUT body under a 0x02 response filename.
It sleeps 30 seconds after each pass. A fully stubbed HTTP/CLR trace verified one
pass and result-body wiring, without network access or executing managed bytes.

PowerShell: the Token parameter authenticates a WebClient. Each loop downloads
and JSON-parses a OneDrive listing, filters 0x01 names, passes DownloadData bytes
directly to Assembly.Load, resolves/invokes the same method, and sends its UTF-8
result with UploadData(..., 'PUT', ...). It sleeps 30 seconds. Substring removes
the task filename suffix when constructing the output URL; it does NOT carve a
delimited downloaded payload. PowerShell method invocations are absent from the
flow projection, so structural queries bind the actual nested calls and arguments.

C#: Main returns unless exactly one token argument is supplied. Store is a
byte-upload helper using PutAsync and ByteArrayContent. Startup sends hostname
and OS version. The 30-second loop dispatches three task types: 0X01 downloads
and invokes a managed assembly then uploads the result as 0X02; 0X03 retrieves
a remotely chosen local path, reads that file asynchronously and uploads it as
0X04; 0X05 parses a remote JSON task, extracts source item and destination path,
downloads item bytes and writes them to that local path, then sends 0X06 status.
Helper-aware structural queries bind the helper name, its byte parameter, the
HTTP-selected read path, actual sent body, and JSON-selected write destination.

Limits: none of the sources contains obfuscation, encoded executable stages,
credential harvesting, durable persistence, cleanup, or security-control bypass.
The selected assemblies themselves are not present; a method name is not proof
of OS shell execution. Tokens, cloud contents, deployment context, and managed
runtime success are unobserved. Python needs Python.NET; PowerShell/.NET runtimes
were unavailable for live execution. Static call/control-flow relationships
establish capabilities; the mocked Python trace establishes only branch wiring.
Each scan contains one source file, with no archive members or fetched dependency
responsible for findings. No dependency-specific exception was added.

Rule changes and coverage
- Extended the existing HTTP-to-Assembly.Load-to-GetMethod.Invoke provenance
  with urllib response reads and bytearray transfer, preserving managed clients.
- Added PowerShell structural HTTP/assembly invocation and hexadecimal suffix
  matching, without requiring particular suffix values, class or method names.
- Added bound PUT result-return detections and a C2 result-return composite.
- Extended existing remotely selected file-upload detection to async reads and
  named byte-upload helpers. Added notable hostname/OS PUT-body and remote-task
  selected file-download destination detections. No execution claim is inferred
  merely from writing the downloaded file.
- Relocated the C# HTTP assembly loader from objectives/command-and-control/
  dropper/module-load to micro-behaviors/process/deploy/module-load, preserving
  its complete matcher and suspicious severity: ordinary plugin hosts can do it.
- Retained the former PowerShell download/string-slicing regex as a notable
  data/string/access observation, with an honest co-occurrence description.
  Download followed by an unrelated filename Substring is not payload carving.
  Its generic decode/load consumer is now a suspicious os/module/load composite:
  the old required evidence never bound downloaded bytes to the assembly and
  did not establish hostile intent. Removed unsupported T1105/T1140 and B0024
  claims from that generic consumer; reflective loading remains represented.
- Corrected the /root filesystem-reference matcher to reject concatenated URL
  suffixes, while preserving standalone absolute paths and mixed URL/FS cases.

Every pre-existing suspicious/hostile fixture finding is retained at the same
severity after mapping the C# loader relocation, except the unsupported
PowerShell delimiter finding. The existing social-shell fixture still reports
its hostile Twitter tasking behavior. The supplied samples lose only that
unsupported delimiter claim, the URL-derived /root filesystem false positive,
and the old ID of the unchanged relocated C# loader. No supported attack loss.

Hostile coverage goal
Python and PowerShell each contain two distinct supported hostile results:
cloud assembly task execution and return of that result. Neither implements
local-file theft or host profiling. The additional download, reflective loading,
HTTP methods, suffix comparison and polling are covered as neutral behaviors;
counting those again as hostile would duplicate task execution or invent intent.
There is no uncovered third hostile effect in their bytes and no matcher limit
preventing detection of the two present effects. C# has three hostile findings:
cloud task execution, result return, and remotely selected file theft. Host
profiling and remote-directed file writing are additionally covered as notable
source-to-sink capabilities.

Validation evidence
22 added positive/near-miss controls pass via check.py, including renamed class,
method, variable/helper and suffix values, local-only modules, overwritten
results/read paths, fixed bodies, non-PUT method, an unopened request, changed
write destination, inert documentation/comments, genuine delimiter decoding,
and standalone/mixed/relative root paths. Existing cloud-managed-tasking fixtures
and the external social-shell and decoded-loader fixtures were rescanned before
and after the changes. The latter is retained as a real extracted-stage control.
No sample or regression fixture was allowed to contact its configured endpoint.

Final local classifier observations (model v18.18; engine 2.13.0)
cloud_tasks.py: H/S 0/0 -> 2/0; ML BENIGN (0.30289346) -> HOSTILE (0.99656284).
cloud_tasks.ps1: H/S 0/1 -> 2/0; ML BENIGN (0.97500200) -> HOSTILE (0.99450296).
cloud_tasks.cs: H/S 1/1 -> 3/1; ML HOSTILE (0.99996200) -> HOSTILE (0.99995870).
The queue's earlier HOSTILE prior did not reproduce in the initial local
Python/PowerShell scans. All final local classifier verdicts now agree with
this review. Atomscan warns that the installed feature spec is v18 while the
engine expects v21; those model inputs were not changed here. Python/C# facts
retain explicit flow-projection limitations, addressed for these paths by
bounded structural queries rather than claiming complete program analysis.
